steps.caption: Same position, shown again. White's rook has one move that attacks the king. Watch what the black king can do afterwards.

line.say: The rook slides up the open file and attacks the king along the back row.

steps.text: **Checkmate** is a check that the king cannot escape. The game ends at once and the side giving it wins. In the last lessons you met the three ways out of check: move the king, capture the checker, or block. Checkmate is the case where all three are impossible. Next, the same mate frozen, so you can see why.

steps.caption: Frozen: Black to move and no legal move. Its own pawns fill the squares in front of the king. The rook's line runs through the king, so h8 is covered too.

steps.text: Before you say checkmate, ask three questions, in a good order. Can the king step to a safe square? Can the checking piece be captured? Can anything be put in between? If all three answers are no, it is checkmate. If two pieces give check at once, only a king move can answer. The mate you just saw is a **back-rank mate**: the back rank is the row where a side's pieces start, and the king's own pawns trap it there.

steps.title: One pawn moved
steps.prompt: Same position, one pawn moved: is Ra8 still mate? Predict first.

steps.caption: After the rook check, the king steps to h7. One pawn move gave it a square to run to, so it was check, not checkmate.

line.say: The king escapes to the square the pawn left free.

steps.caption: A second way out of a back-rank check: a block. The knight can jump between the rook and the king.

line.say: The rook checks along the back row.
The knight jumps in between. It is check answered, not mate.

steps.caption: A third way out: capture. Black has a rook on the back row, and the white rook is not defended.

line.say: The rook checks along the back row.
Black's rook takes it. The check is gone and White has lost its rook.

steps.caption: The queen checks from the square next to the black king. The white king also defends that square, so Black cannot take her.

line.say: The queen arrives next to the king. The white king defends her, so she cannot be taken.

steps.caption: Same queen move, but White's king is far away. Nothing defends the queen, so the black king captures her.

line.say: The queen checks, but she stands alone.
The king takes the queen. White has lost her for nothing.

steps.title: Helped or alone?
steps.prompt: Same queen, same black king, only White's king moved. Predict first: mate in both?

steps.caption: The queen went to g6 instead. Black is not in check and has no legal move. That is **stalemate**: a draw, not a win.

steps.text: Two rooks can mate with no help from pawns. One rook cuts off a whole row so the king cannot step onto it; the other checks along the edge row. Neither rook needs defending because the king cannot get near either.

steps.caption: Two rooks take turns. Whatever the king does on the back row, Ra8 is mate. Try Kh8 yourself.

line.say: The first rook takes the seventh row. This is not check, but the king cannot step onto that row.
The king can only shuffle along the back row.
The second rook checks. The first rook covers the row in front, so the king has no square.

steps.text: The queen can also be defended by a **bishop**. At the start of a game the pawn on f7 is guarded only by the king. If the queen and a bishop both aim there, the queen takes with check and the king cannot take back. Watch how a short game reaches that position.

steps.caption: A short game. The pawn on f7 is attacked twice by White and defended once, by the king.

line.say: White opens in the centre.
Black matches it.
The queen comes out and looks at the pawn on f7.
Black develops but does not notice the target.
The bishop comes out and aims at the same pawn.
Black attacks the queen and forgets about f7.

steps.caption: Now the queen takes. The bishop defends her, so the king cannot take her. d7, d8 and f8 hold Black's own pieces and the queen herself covers e7.

line.say: The queen takes with check. Checkmate: the bishop defends her.

steps.caption: Same idea, but the bishop is on b5 and does not aim at f7. The queen takes with check, and the king simply takes her.

line.say: The queen takes with check.
The king takes her. Nothing defended f7.

steps.caption: How does Black stop it? The queen and bishop both aim at f7. Defend it once more, or chase the queen away.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen, so she must move. The threat is gone.

steps.text: [I] Inference from the position: defend f7 once more (...Qe7 or ...Nh6) or chase the queen (...g6) and the mate disappears. Decent opponents do this, so treat the quick queen-and-bishop attack as a trap for careless players, not a plan.

A knight checks by jumping, so nothing can be put in its way. The defender may capture the knight or move the king. In a **smothered** mate the king's own pieces take away its squares and nothing can capture the knight: the king is boxed in by its own side.

steps.caption: The black king on a8 has a pawn on a7, a pawn on b7 and a rook on b8 around it.

line.say: The knight jumps to c7 and attacks the king. Its own pieces box the king in, and nothing can take the knight.

steps.caption: Remove the rook and the king has b8.

line.say: The knight checks.
The king steps to b8, the square the rook used to fill.

steps.text: When you look for mate, make a list of every check first. Then run the three questions on each. [H] My guess: most checks in a position are not mate, so listing them all beats stopping at the first. Next, one position with three checks: only one finishes the game.

Emanuel Lasker, in *Common Sense in Chess*, counted squares: a mate needs the king's own square and each neighbour controlled or blocked by the king's own pieces, up to nine, with the checking piece safe. [H] My guess, not a tested fact: beginners miss mates because they check one exit and stop. Say the three questions out loud every time.

steps.caption: White has three checks. The queen can go to e8, a8 or h7. Think about each before the next steps show it.
First check: a8. The black rook can block it.

line.say: The queen checks along the back row.
The rook blocks. Check answered, no mate.

steps.caption: Second check: h7. The queen takes a pawn, and the rook on h3 defends her. Still, the king has a square.

line.say: The queen takes on h7 with check. The white rook defends her.
The king steps away.

steps.caption: Third check: e8. The black rook cannot reach e8 or f8, and the pawns fill the king's squares.

line.say: The queen checks and the king has no square. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Now the other side. White's rook threatens a mate. Black to move: what can the defender do?

line.say: The pawn steps up. The king now has a square to run to.

steps.caption: After the pawn move, the same rook check is no longer mate.

line.say: The rook checks.
The king steps to the square the pawn left free.

steps.caption: Another defence: ...g6 gives the king g7. Re8+ is answered by Kg7.

line.say: The rook checks.
The king has a square.

steps.text: A flight square made for the king is called **luft**. [I] My judgement, untested: ...h6 and ...g6 are the usual cheap ways to make luft, because they weaken few squares; ...f6 loosens the king more. Try each in the lab before you trust this.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend why Re8 is mate in the first position but not when Black's h-pawn stands on h6. Use the words step, capture and block.

steps.text: **A model answer.** In the first position the king cannot step (its own pawns fill f7, g7 and h7, the rook covers f8 and h8), nothing can capture the rook, and nothing can block. With the pawn on h6 the king can step to h7, so it is only check. The shapes to look for: a back-rank mate, a queen defended by her king or a bishop, two rooks, and a smothered knight.

steps.prompt: Think of the last position where you were tempted by a check that was not mate. Which of the three questions would have caught it: step, capture or block?
